the cytomorphologic changes in the respiratory tract of dogs exposed to BP and NMU are characteristic for each carcinogens and that the cytologic findings are consistent with the histologic lesions observed in these dogs.
the cytologic changes induced by BP and NMU were distinct and characteristic, and that the cytologic pattern of NMU was more prominent than that of BP in the early stage of carcinogenesis.
the early cytologic changes induced by chemical carcinogens in the canine respiratory mucosa were characteristic for each chemical carcinogen.

the cytologic correlates of chemical agents in the respiratory tract.
the cytologic correlates of chemical respiratory carcinogens in dogs and the use of cytology to evaluate carcinogen-induced changes.
the use of cytology as a means to monitor chemical carcinogenesis in the respiratory tract of the dog.

NMU and BP induce different cytologic patterns of change in canine bronchial and bronchiolar epithelium, and that the cytologic patterns induced by the two chemicals are distinct and reproducible.

the cytologic findings of cells in respiratory tract carcinogenesis studies in dogs are consistent with the carcinogen employed and are useful as a means of monitoring the effects of carcinogens in vivo.

the cytomorphologic changes in respiratory epithelium are specific and characteristic for each carcinogenic agent and that these cytologic changes are useful in the early detection of carcinogen-induced respiratory tract lesions in dogs.

cytomorphology of the respiratory tract can be used to predict carcinogen exposure.
